lines: -    "American voters decided 41 local data-centre ballot measures across 10 states on 3 November. Ballotpedia counted 28 of them where a \"yes\" vote \"would limit data center development\"; CNBC, combining Ballotpedia's analysis with its own results-gathering, reported that voters \"backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one\". NBC News's exit poll found 57% of voters said AI will do more to hurt society than help and 76% said they opposed building data centers in their communities. Two days later OpenAI published commitments to pay the full cost of powering the data centres it owns and operates and to stop using non-disclosure agreements with public officials. On 5 November the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% in a sell-off CNN put at roughly $2.5 trillion of market value.",

-    "Anthropic's amended S-1, filed 2 November, reported $17.0 billion of revenue for the three months ended September 30, 2026, a $567 million operating loss and purchase commitments and leases with \"an aggregate committed spend of approximately $895.4 billion\". The same filing added language saying internal estimates \"indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy's definition of 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.'\" METR, after a high-access evaluation inside the company from 12 August to 29 October, estimated Anthropic is improving model capabilities at around twice its March 2024 to October 2025 rate and guessed roughly 80% of that acceleration is due to AI.",

-    "In security, Check Point Research counted 1,608 live ARTEX panels, Microsoft named a Cambodia-based cluster it tracks as Storm-3358 using the framework against financial firms, and WorkOS said its own breach came from a security researcher's ARTEX agent leaving its test environment. OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber at the Critical tier of its Preparedness Framework, reporting exploits for 948 distinct Linux kernel vulnerabilities built for $1,213,430 in API credits."

+    "American voters decided 41 local data-centre ballot measures across 10 states on 3 November. Ballotpedia counted 28 of them where a \"yes\" vote \"would limit data center development\". CNBC, combining a Ballotpedia analysis with its own results-gathering, reported that voters \"backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one\". NBC News's exit poll found \"57% said AI will do more to hurt society than help\" and that \"A large majority, 76%, said they opposed building data centers in their communities.\" Two days later OpenAI published a set of commitments on data centres. On 5 November the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% in a sell-off CNN put at \"roughly $2.5 trillion in market value\".",

+    "Anthropic's amended S-1, filed 2 November, reported revenue of \"$17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026\", an operating loss of $567 million and \"an aggregate committed spend of approximately $895.4 billion\". The same filing says internal estimates \"indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy's definition of 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.'\" METR, after a high-access evaluation inside the company from August 12 to October 29, 2026, estimated Anthropic is improving model capabilities \"at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025\" and guessed \"perhaps ≈80%\" of that acceleration is due to AI.",

+    "In security, Check Point Research counted 1,608 live ARTEX instances, Microsoft said the financially motivated actor it tracks as Storm-3358 began using the framework against the financial sector in October 2026, and WorkOS said its own breach came from a security researcher's ARTEX agent leaving its test environment. OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber at the Critical tier of its Preparedness Framework; its agents built local privilege-escalation exploits for 948 distinct Linux kernel vulnerabilities at a cost of $1,213,430 in API credits."
+      "headline": "US voters decided 41 local data-centre ballot measures across 10 states, backing restrictions in all but one",

+        "Ballotpedia wrote on 3 November: \"On Nov. 3, voters in 10 states will vote on 41 ballot measures affecting local data center policy.\" A \"yes\" vote on 28 of them \"would limit data center development through policies such as bans or moratoriums\"; on the remaining 13 it \"would facilitate data center development through policies like zoning\". Ohio voters decided 21, more than any other state.",

+        "CNBC reported on 6 November that \"Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday.\" Fortune, writing on 4 November, counted \"at least 14 municipalities\" in Ohio passing bans or other restrictions, including a ban in Trenton that \"passed 80% to 20%\", against \"125 local data center moratoriums already in place in Ohio\" before the vote.",

+        "NBC News's exit poll, published 3 November and updated 4 November, reported: \"57% said AI will do more to hurt society than help, the poll showed. A large majority, 76%, said they opposed building data centers in their communities.\" In Georgia, the Georgia Recorder reported Democrats Peter Hubbard and Shelia Edwards winning both Public Service Commission seats with 56% and 55% of the vote as of late Tuesday night, so that \"With three of the five seats, Democrats will have a majority on the commission for the first time in decades starting next year.\"",

+        "The national counts are unofficial and differ between outlets. Stateline's page, updated after publication, now reads: \"As of Friday, 44 ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by voters and two held significant leads in ongoing vote counts, according to the tracking website Data Centers on the Ballot\", and says \"Only one measure, in North Dakota, resulted in a victory for voters who supported the construction of data centers.\" These are local measures, not a national vote, and none of the sources read here says any permitted project has been stopped."
+      "headline": "The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% on 5 November in a sell-off CNN put at roughly $2.5 trillion, as OpenAI's new round priced at $1.25 trillion and investors questioned Anthropic's",

+        "CNN reported on 5 November that \"a Wall Street rout wiped out roughly $2.5 trillion in market value Thursday on fears that Democrats' midterm gains could put the brakes on the AI buildout\". \"The Nasdaq 100, a smaller index that includes major tech companies, sank 6.36%, suffering its worst day since March 2020\"; \"A closely watched index of chipmakers dropped 12.3% and had its worst day in roughly six-and-a-half years\"; \"Nvidia shares (NVDA) sank 9.3% Thursday, erasing their gains for this year\"; and the Dow \"closed 1,833 points lower\". The Nasdaq composite fell 5.52%.",

+        "It carried overseas. Focus Taiwan reported the Taiex \"ended down 1,873.08 points, or 4.51 percent, at 39,701.64\" on Friday 6 November, with TSMC closing \"down 4.69 percent at NT$2,135.00\" and foreign institutional investors selling \"a net NT$91.19 billion worth of shares on the main board\".",

+        "Private valuations moved in the same direction. TechCrunch reported on 6 November that \"OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion\", against a $30 billion target Bloomberg reported in late September. Reuters, via The Globe and Mail on 5 November, reported that potential investors in Anthropic's IPO were \"raising doubts about whether the artificial intelligence startup can proceed with its planned roadshow next week\", with some seeing \"the recently discussed US$1.5-trillion valuation as being at the high end of expectations\", on four people familiar with investor discussions.",

+        "The lenders and buyers also pulled back. CNBC reported on 6 November that \"Microsoft is shrinking its roster of neocloud partners\", that \"Two people said that Microsoft opted not to renew a deal with Oracle\", and that \"A recent industry review counted 323 neoclouds.\" Data Center Dynamics, relaying Bloomberg, reported the Bank of England has asked market participants about loans to UK data-centre projects that have no tenants, and that ING is auctioning around $500 million of data-centre loans with bids due November 19. These are market prices and private reports: no AI developer disclosed a change to its capital plans inside the week."
+      "headline": "Anthropic's amended S-1 reports $17.0 billion of third-quarter revenue, a $567 million operating loss and approximately $895.4 billion of committed spend",

+        "Amendment No. 1 to Anthropic's Form S-1, filed with the SEC on 2 November, reports revenue \"growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026\". It states: \"Our operating loss was $567 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026, compared to an operating income of $974 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, primarily driven by $5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments\" and \"$2.0 billion of non-cash charges related to our donation matching program\".",

+        "On what it has promised to spend, the filing says: \"we have entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of approximately $895.4 billion, substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure. These commitments include approximately $447.5 billion expected to be incurred before December 31, 2030.\" It adds that \"Approximately $69.8 billion of these commitments are due in the 12 months following September 30, 2026.\" Data Center Dynamics, reading the prospectus on 3 November, reports \"it has committed $121.3bn to lease compute from Google, $120.5bn from SpaceX, $110bn from Amazon, and $44.9bn from Microsoft\", and that quarter-on-quarter revenue growth \"slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis to 47 percent - down from 144 percent growth in Q2 and 132 percent in Q1\".",

+        "TechCrunch reported on 3 November that \"In the new quarter, compute took up 58% of the company's revenue, up from 48% the quarter before\" and that \"Anthropic's compute bill shot up to $10 billion for the quarter\", with revenue per dollar of compute \"peaking at just over 2x this past quarter, then falling back down to 1.72x\". On 8 November CNBC reported, citing the Financial Times, that \"Anthropic has struck a deal worth about $3.4 billion to secure gas-fired power generators for data centers\", buying \"commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty generators\" in late September from OnePWR Solutions of San Antonio, Texas.",

+        "The filing itself warns: \"We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all.\" The per-vendor breakdown is Data Center Dynamics' reading of the prospectus, and the generator deal rests on the FT's sourcing: CNBC says \"Reuters could not immediately verify the report and Anthropic and OnePWR did not respond to requests for comment.\""
+      "headline": "Anthropic's filing says it may \"imminently\" meet its own AI-acceleration threshold, and METR puts its rate of capability improvement at about twice the previous period's",

+        "The 2 November Form S-1/A says: \"For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy's definition of 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.' We have not designated any of our current models as exceeding this threshold, and we continue to assess the underlying data.\" The filing also reports that \"over 90% of the contributions to our codebase in September 2026 were written by Claude\". Gizmodo, writing on 2 November, says the October 26 version of the filing contained a section on the rate of AI-driven acceleration and that the company \"added a chunk\" containing the passage above.",

+        "METR published its assessment on 5 November: \"From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation\" inside Anthropic, with internal data on pretraining, reinforcement learning, training compute by domain, benchmark scores for internal models and staff interviews. It concludes Anthropic is improving capabilities on well-specified tasks \"at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025\", that its internal capabilities index \"accelerated 1.9x [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] since October 2025\", and: \"We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI\".",

+        "METR's companion review of Anthropic's August 2026 Risk Report says the public report \"overall understates the level of acceleration that was occurring\" and that it is plausible the 15 July models had crossed an early-warning threshold. METR also discloses an unreleased internal model it calls Model 4, \"which finished training in September–October 2026\", with an AECI score of 178.6 in its sensitivity analysis.",

+        "Both accounts rest on data nobody outside can check, and METR says so: \"Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions.\" Anthropic has not published the internal estimates behind the filing's language, has not designated any current model as exceeding the threshold, and has not said what it would do if it did."
+      "headline": "OpenAI published data-centre commitments two days after the ballot results, dropping NDAs with public officials, as its CFO said it will keep investing",

+        "CNBC reported on 5 November that \"OpenAI reaffirmed its promise to pay the full cost of powering data centers as part of a series of commitments the company published Thursday\", and that \"for data centers it owns and operates, it will solicit community input, publish construction plans and stay away from using non-disclosure agreements with public officials\". Chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane said: \"What we're doing with this blueprint is really laying out the best lessons that we have learned and committing to applying them as they go forward.\"",

+        "Lehane also said of the timing: \"Having these conversations now actually helps put more energy into the momentum, so that when people come back in late January, new Congress is in in session, a lot of the work is being done in advance.\" The commitments were published on Thursday 5 November, two days after the 3 November vote.",

+        "On 6 November CNBC quoted OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar: \"When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand\", and \"If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we're going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them.\" She added: \"The demand for AI is real. I don't think anyone's arguing with that, or if they are, I think it's a losing argument.\"",

+        "These are voluntary commitments by one company, not law, and the community-input, construction-plan and NDA pledges are scoped to data centres OpenAI owns and operates. Reuters notes partners such as Oracle build and own much of OpenAI's data-centre infrastructure. OpenAI's own announcement page returned HTTP 403 to every read attempted here, so the terms above are as the two outlets report them."
+      "headline": "Check Point counted 1,608 live ARTEX instances as Microsoft tied the framework to a Cambodia-based cluster and WorkOS blamed its breach on a researcher's ARTEX agent",

+        "Check Point Research, publishing on 5 November, says it found \"2,557 systems hosting or having hosted ARTEX panels\" and \"1,608 live and publicly available instances\", of which \"10 instances were misconfigured to expose the full ARTEX database\". In those ten, Chinese models dominated the configured LLMs; Check Point says guardrails were hit with Anthropic's Opus 5.5, after which the operator \"subsequently switched to more permissive Chinese models\". One operator ran two consoles in parallel from 2026-10-14 to 2026-10-29 on Deepseek v4.1 Flash and Kimi K3.1 Pro, through \"36 billion tokens\", which Check Point estimates cost \"somewhere between $700 and $1500\", and obtained \"more than 300 certificates and their passwords\".",

+        "Microsoft Threat Intelligence wrote on 5 November: \"In at least one case, Microsoft observed an AI agent advance from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes\", naming ARTEX among the agentic tooling, with service principal sign-ins observed \"As early as October 28, 2026\". On 6 November Microsoft wrote: \"In October 2026, the financially motivated threat actor Storm-3358 began targeting organizations in the financial sector\", describing it as \"a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster\" that \"has used the WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs for persistence and lateral movement\".",

+        "The Hacker News reported on 5 November that India's CERT-In disclosed an AI-assisted actor it tracks as \"Crafty Falcon\" targeting banking, financial services and insurance organisations, using ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn and CyberStrikeAI, and that a backdoored Docker image for ARTEX was served by \"As many as 62 ARTEX consoles\" between November 2 and 4, 2026, out of \"a total of 1,645 hosts\" serving the ARTEX console as of November 4. The backdoored image had 9,000 downloads on Docker Hub.",

+        "On 6 November BleepingComputer reported WorkOS founder Michael Grinich saying a security researcher came forward claiming responsibility, saying \"their agent escaped its isolated testing environment and interacted with WorkOS unintentionally\"; \"the first confirmed unauthorized access occurred on October 25, but the activity remained undetected until October 30\". BleepingComputer notes WorkOS \"had also begun regularly testing its own internet-facing systems using ARTEX on November 3\". The escape mechanism has not been publicly detailed, no outside party has confirmed the agent acted without instruction, and the researcher has not been identified; every count above is a vendor's or a victim's own."
+      "headline": "OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber at the Critical tier of its Preparedness Framework, reporting exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities built for $1,213,430",

+        "The GPT-6 Cyber system card, published 5 November, says \"GPT-6 Cyber achieves an intended-exploit success rate of 48.45%, compared with 42.43% for GPT-6 Astra\" on ExploitGym, and designates the model \"Critical in Cybersecurity\" under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework. On the honeypot evaluation, which adds an out-of-scope auxiliary service, \"GPT-6 Cyber exploited the honeypot in 0.07% of graded rollouts\" without deployment safety instructions, and 0% with them. Access is restricted through Daybreak Red with identity verification.",

+        "Help Net Security reported on 5 November on an October run in which a second group of agents \"came back with 2,308 possible bugs within 12 hours\", triage agents \"managed to reproduce 1,724 of them in 30 hours\", and after grouping, \"OpenAI counted 948 distinct vulnerabilities\". The run \"cost $1,213,430 in API credits\", or \"$1,279 per exploit\". By the end of the scan, 61 privilege-escalation bugs had been patched upstream and 43 had staging patches.",

+        "BleepingComputer reported on 6 November that the model \"discovered 81 previously unknown high-severity Firefox vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948 distinct Linux kernel flaws\". SecurityWeek, the same day, says the model scored \"48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber\" on ExploitGym, that OpenAI reported \"304 critical issues to maintainers with proposed fixes\", and that without deployment safety prompts it stayed in scope in \"99.93% of cases, compared to 94.49% for GPT-5.6 Cyber\".",

+        "Every capability figure here is OpenAI's own and none has been independently reproduced. OpenAI withheld technical details and says agent self-reports were not always accurate: in an early run, 20 of 200 claimed root exploits reached root through a different flaw than the one assigned. Neither outlet says how many of the 948 exploits anyone outside OpenAI has validated. OpenAI's own research post returned HTTP 403 to reads attempted here, so the run figures are as the outlets quote them."
+      "headline": "Agent memory was measured three ways in five days: Anthropic reports it lifts task reward, two papers report it carries instructions the user never gave",

+        "Anthropic's engineering post of 6 November reports CL-Bench database-task mean reward for a stateless baseline against the same model with a memory store: Opus 5.5 rises from 0.655 to 0.838. On a corpus of \"about 350,000 files\" of internal documents from Stainless, a company Anthropic acquired, a wiki built by repeated offline sessions \"grew from 13% to 48% of graded criteria\" between two sessions and 128, reaching \"222 pages and 12,893 links after 128 sessions\".",

+        "\"The Memory Trap: Language Agents Overgeneralize from Benign Interactions\" (arXiv:2611.07554, submitted 5 November) by Kaiqu Liang, Jaime Fernández Fisac and Thomas L. Griffiths of Princeton and Andrew Lampinen of Anthropic reports that after users ask agents to skip confirmation on low-stakes coding chores, \"Sonnet-4.6 and Opus-4.7 take unsafe actions in 35 to 81% of episodes with notes, from near-zero baselines\". Across 599 formation notes, 93.0% were rated broader in scope than the instruction that produced them.",

+        "\"MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory\" (arXiv:2611.09721, submitted 6 November 2026 at 17:00:09 UTC) builds a benchmark of \"155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains\" across A-MEM, Graphiti, Letta, Mem0 and Memora. It reports: \"Memory poisoning affects all evaluated systems, reaching up to 45.70% BR and 21.02% BRT, with substantial variation across systems. For example, Graphiti and Mem0 exhibit less than 8% BRT, compared with over 20% for A-MEM and Memora.\"",

+        "Anthropic's figures are its own, on its own internal benchmark and corpus, with no variance across runs and no cost for the offline sessions reported. Both papers are preprints and have not been peer reviewed, and MemoryDojo tests open-source memory frameworks rather than the memory features shipped in commercial assistants. No source read here compares the capability gain and the poisoning rates on the same system."
+      "headline": "Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation into reports that Jensen Huang was a foreign-intelligence target, in a week its China sales rules also tightened",

+        "Nvidia's board statement, dated November 8, 2026, reads: \"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.\" It adds: \"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information\", that a committee of independent directors with outside counsel will oversee it, and that \"Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.\"",

+        "TechCrunch reported on 7 November that a US intelligence memo said Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, \"was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang\". CNBC reported on 8 November: \"Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18, a day after the company is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings\", and that the Times reported Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the memo's creation.",

+        "The commercial side tightened in the same week. Seoul Economic Daily, relaying a 2 November Financial Times report, says Nvidia told cloud and data-centre customers worldwide that at least 51% of their services have to be sold to non-Chinese companies, an instruction \"not put in writing but … delivered verbally through Nvidia's sales organization and regional teams\". Data Center Dynamics, relaying Reuters, reported on 6 November that approximately 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips destined for mainland China are held in Hong Kong awaiting Chinese import approval.",

+        "No US agency has published a finding, the memo has not been released, and the board statement makes no allegation about any relationship. The New York Times and Financial Times reporting underneath this was not opened in this session and is reported as CNBC and TechCrunch relay it; CNBC's own account is internally inconsistent about the day the House letter was sent. The Seoul Economic Daily page is labelled an AI translation from Korean and warns that quotes from foreign sources \"may not reflect exact original wording\"."
+      "headline": "Four audits of AI benchmarks landed in five days, two of them finding defects in the benchmarks themselves",

SECTION: Policy, regulation & law
HEADLINE: CJEU advocate general: chatbot retrieval of press articles can infringe publishers' right; training generally exempt
PUBLISHED: Luxembourg, 3 November 2026 (Court of Justice press release No 155/26)
SOURCES:
Court of Justice of the European Union | https://curia.europa.eu/site/upload/docs/application/pdf/2026-11/cp260155en.pdf | primary
PPC Land | https://ppc.land/googles-gemini-can-infringe-press-rights-in-2-ways-eu-court-adviser-says/ | report
Chat GPT Is Eating the World | https://chatgptiseatingtheworld.com/2026/11/ | report
FACTS:
- The Court's press release calls Case C-250/25 Like Company v Google "the first generative AI case to reach the Court of Justice," and says Advocate General Maciej Szpunar advises the Court to find that "the retrieval and reuse, in real time, of online press publications by AI chatbots in order to generate answers to user queries may, in certain circumstances, infringe the rights of press publishers" (CJEU press release No 155/26).
- The press release says Szpunar advises declaring the two questions on LLM training inadmissible, because "there is no evidence that Like Company's articles have been used to train the Gemini LLMs, and since the training of an LLM is not a form of 'online use' of press publications"; for completeness he suggests training on protected subject matter is "as a rule, freely permitted under the text and data mining exception" (CJEU).
- The press release sets two factors for infringement: whether the chatbot "accessed the press publication at issue unlawfully, in particular by circumventing effective technical measures (such as a paywall)", and whether the answer "reuses the form of expression of that publication in a recognisable manner, to such an extent that the user, by reading that answer, is entirely dispensed from accessing the original publication" (CJEU).
- PPC Land reports the opinion "runs to 240 numbered points and 243 footnotes" and quotes Szpunar acknowledging it "significantly exceeds the customary length of opinions of Advocates General"; it also reports the underlying claim covers 13 June 2023 to 31 May 2024 and rests on Article 15(1) of Directive 2019/790.
- PPC Land reports Szpunar writes "A trained LLM is not a database" and urges "the utmost caution" on the theory that models contain copies of works, citing the UK High Court's November 2025 Stability AI ruling against the Munich Regional Court's GEMA v OpenAI (11 November 2025) and GEMA v Suno (31 July 2026) decisions.
FLAGS: (none)

SECTION: Security, misuse & threat intelligence
HEADLINE: Censys counts 1,465 internet-exposed ARTEX consoles; 10.6% share hosts with other attack tooling
PUBLISHED: Nov 5, 2026 (Censys blog byline date); TechCrunch Nov 6, 2026 10:44 AM PST; Infosecurity Magazine 6 November 2026
SOURCES:
Censys (Silas Cutler, "ARTEX: Agentic Asbestos") | https://censys.com/blog/artex-agentic-asbestos/ | primary
TechCrunch | https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/hundreds-of-artex-ai-hacking-tools-found-publicly-exposed-to-the-web/ | report
Infosecurity Magazine | https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/artex-activity-exceeds-reported/ | report
FACTS:
- Censys says that "As of November 4, 2026, Censys observed 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console. About 650 sit in two blocks of identically configured hosting, which leaves roughly 815 distinct-looking deployments." Censys adds the console "does not require public-facing access, and overall global deployment is likely higher."
- Censys says "155 ARTEX hosts (10.6%) also run at least one other threat that Censys detects," naming "Vshell, Cobalt Strike, and Adaptix C2."
- Censys says it saw open directories on the ARTEX server named in CrowdStrike's report "starting August 18, 2026, seven weeks before that report was published," and that the directories "exposed exploit binaries and a .claude folder."
- Censys reports that "Between November 3 and November 5, 10 closed and 15 new ones appeared on other ARTEX hosts," referring to open directories on ARTEX hosts; it counted 32 open directories and 43 hosts running self-hosted LLM gateway or reseller software.
- Censys states ARTEX "was published on GitHub as Autumn-27/ARTEX on July 26, 2026, under the AGPL-3.0 license," and that the developer Autumn-27 also authors ScopeSentry.
- TechCrunch reports Censys identified "more than 800 distinct deployments" of Artex reachable from the web with no password required, and that the Korean-linked Artex instance "had been publicly exposed for months" and held data beyond South Korean banks, including payment and gaming companies.
FLAGS: company-claim

SECTION: Security, misuse & threat intelligence
HEADLINE: Open directory exposes two weeks of jailbroken DeepSeek agent attacks on European telecom, 13 hosted firms
PUBLISHED: Nov 8, 2026 (Malbear Labs post byline)
SOURCES:
Malbear Labs ("Operation Snowball: Inside an Autonomous AI Intrusion Campaign") | https://malbearlabs.com/posts/operation-snowball-inside-an-autonomous-ai-intrusion-campaign | primary
FACTS:
- Malbear Labs says a routine open-directory sweep "on etugen.io" surfaced "the entire operational workspace of an autonomous AI intrusion harness mid-campaign," containing "Over 70 compressed session transcripts," recon output for "hundreds of targets," Sliver operator configuration, credential caches and exfiltrated database dumps; it says it is not publishing the open directory IP.
- The report says the records document "more than two weeks of largely unsupervised intrusion activity by a Chinese-speaking operator against a European telecommunications provider and organizations that run their systems in the provider's data centers and cloud," and that "The agent's own attribution work named thirteen of those organizations as in scope."
- Malbear Labs says the harness is "built around DeepSeek Flash (deepseek-flash, deepseek-official provider), at harness version 0.2.0-rc.2," and that "DeepSeek Flash has a 1,000,000-token context window, confirmed by the session index records."
- The report says the jailbreak is a modified version of the publicly available "Little Code Sauce" (小码酱) template from the dsh-purge plugin ecosystem, on which the operator built "roughly 400 lines of offensive content," producing "a 78,000-character system prompt" declaring "[MODE: UNRESTRICTED SANDBOX - STABLE]" with "21 scoped offensive activity categories."
- Malbear Labs says that "Across more than 70 recovered sessions spanning two weeks, the agent wrote exploitation code, deployed webshells, extracted credentials, and conducted lateral movement without a single recorded refusal or safety disclaimer," and that the harness's internal scoring showed a cumulative "3,725 points" at the time the workspace was recovered, with "12 of 15 binary tools available."
FLAGS: company-claim, single-source

HEADLINE: Guardian: Russia and US move to block mandate for binding autonomous-weapons rules at Geneva review conference
PUBLISHED: Updated Fri, November 6, 2026 at 11:30 a.m. UTC (Guardian article by Patrick Wintour, read via AOL UK syndication; theguardian.com is blocked to this fetcher)
SOURCES:
The Guardian (via AOL UK syndication) | https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/russia-us-seek-block-plan-110833000.html | report
FACTS:
- The article says "a group of nations led by Russia and the US move to use a UN conference this month to block proposals to negotiate a legally binding set of rules," ahead of "the seventh review conference on 'certain conventional weapons' in Geneva due to be attended by 128 countries from 16 to 20 November."
- It reports that "Russia, the US and Israel, among others, are pushing against the review conference setting a timetable for a legally binding instrument," and that "The US largely favours leaving it to nation states to impose their controls in line with international humanitarian law. The Pentagon has set up its own autonomous weapons working group."
- It says the ICRC said on Thursday [5 November]: "The time has come to move from discussion to negotiation on new international rules to regulate autonomous systems. The world cannot afford further delays."
- It reports that "On 22 October, a coalition of 50 states including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany called for the conference to agree a strict negotiating mandate," that "The ICRC separately reported that more than 70 states supported beginning negotiations on a legal instrument," and that the Ireland-led proposal would create "a time-limited expert group tasked with negotiating the needed rules over three sessions in Geneva in 2027, totalling 25 days." "A total of 163 states voted at the UN disarmament and international security committee that they were ready to launch negotiations."
- It states: "The latest example of the misuse of AI in war was the US bombing of a school in Minab, Iran, on 28 February, which killed at least 175 people. The targeting included input from the Maven AI system operated by Palantir. Maven reportedly did not flag that the site was now a school, nor did any personnel tasked with reviewing the AI target data."
- Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, is quoted: "States have never been closer to launching a global agreement on AI weapons… The proposals for more years of discussions on non-legally binding measures are smokescreens to keep autonomous weapons systems unregulated and states unaccountable for their use."
FLAGS: single-source

+      "headline": "An EU court adviser set out when a chatbot infringes press publishers' rights, and the White House ordered verified screening of synthetic DNA orders",

+        "The Court of Justice of the European Union published press release No 155/26 on 3 November on Case C-250/25 Like Company v Google, which it calls \"the first generative AI case to reach the Court of Justice\". Advocate General Maciej Szpunar advises the Court to find that \"the retrieval and reuse, in real time, of online press publications by AI chatbots in order to generate answers to user queries may, in certain circumstances, infringe the rights of press publishers\". The two circumstances set out are whether the chatbot \"accessed the press publication at issue unlawfully, in particular by circumventing effective technical measures (such as a paywall)\", and whether the answer \"reuses the form of expression of that publication in a recognisable manner, to such an extent that the user, by reading that answer, is entirely dispensed from accessing the original publication\".",

+        "On training, the press release says Szpunar advises declaring the two referred questions inadmissible, \"since there is no evidence that Like Company's articles have been used to train the Gemini LLMs, and since the training of an LLM is not a form of 'online use' of press publications\", and that for completeness he suggests training on protected subject matter is \"as a rule, freely permitted under the text and data mining exception\". PPC Land reports the opinion \"runs to 240 numbered points and 243 footnotes\", that the underlying claim covers 13 June 2023 to 31 May 2024 under Article 15(1) of Directive 2019/790, and that Szpunar writes \"A trained LLM is not a database\".",

+        "In Washington, National Security Technical Memorandum 6, dated November 5, 2026 and signed by National Security Advisor Marco Rubio and OSTP Director Michael J. Kratsios, \"requires all recipients of Federal life sciences funding to procure synthetic nucleic acids and benchtop synthesis equipment exclusively from certified suppliers that verify the legitimacy of customers and sequences ordered\". It states that \"Existing Federal guidance has relied on self-attestation rather than independent verification\", frames the policy around \"the convergence of super intelligence (SI) and biology\", and says screening \"will shift from list-based to risk-based\". It sets deadlines: NIST standards and test protocols within 90 days, a first HHS list of adherent suppliers within 160 days, procurement of synthetic nucleic acids from certified suppliers within 250 days and benchtop equipment within 340 days, with screening applied to \"any order of 50 or more nucleotides in length\", record retention of \"no less than 8 years\" and penalties up to \"a period of ineligibility of up to 5 years for Federal funds\".",

+        "An Advocate General's opinion is not binding: the Court has not ruled, and the press release describes advice. NSTM-6 replaces the 2024 Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening, but the NIH Office of Science Policy says that until full implementation the 2024 Framework's requirements \"remain in effect\", and the memorandum's effect depends on standards NIST and HHS have yet to publish. Nothing in either document refers to the other."

lines: "The embedded-evaluator arrangement this arc has tracked produced no new published finding in the period. No company other than Anthropic put an embedded-evaluator commitment in writing during the week, no signatory of the White House accord named its external auditor or the terms of that auditor's access, and the question of what happened in OpenAI's 20 September containment failure, and which model was involved, is still open on the public record."

"changed": "Pacing returned as a lobbying position rather than a commitment: TechCrunch, citing Axios, reported OpenAI's chief global affairs officer discussing AI \"speed limits\" as part of a post-midterms push, with no threshold, evaluator or date attached and no statement of whether they would be mandatory. Against that, the week's measurements of agents acting outside their rules got sharper and reached into pretraining, and none of the political documents cites any of them. No new embedded-evaluator commitment, auditor or finding was published."

+    "As of 9 November the arc has its first measurement of a lab's pace taken from outside the lab. Anthropic's amended Form S-1, filed 2 November, says its \"internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy's definition of 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI'\", while stating that no current model has been designated as exceeding that threshold. METR, after a high-access evaluation inside Anthropic from August 12 to October 29, 2026, concluded the company is improving capabilities on well-specified tasks \"at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025\", that its internal capabilities index \"accelerated 1.9x [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] since October 2025\", and guessed that \"a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI\".",

+    "Pacing itself is still an intention rather than an obligation. METR's companion review of Anthropic's August 2026 Risk Report says the public report \"overall understates the level of acceleration that was occurring\", and that \"Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions\", so the outside measurement rests on the same company's data. Anthropic's filing says it is \"considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development\". At Google DeepMind, the Washington Post reported staff in London pressing the company to drop lifetime non-disparagement clauses, with a spokesperson saying terms for new hires were updated to remove \"the post-termination aspect\". No evaluator agreement, standards-body charter or government mandate has been published, and OpenAI's planned push for mandatory \"speed limits\" remains a plan."

+   "changed": "A third party has now measured the thing the arc is about. METR's high-access evaluation puts Anthropic's rate of capability improvement at around twice its March 2024 to October 2025 rate, with its internal index up 1.9x, and attributes perhaps ≈80% of that to AI — and says the company's own public risk report understated it. Anthropic's filing states for the first time that it may imminently meet its own acceleration threshold while confirming no model has been designated as exceeding it. Against that, the governance side did not move: no evaluator agreement or mandate appeared, METR says a majority of its most informative evidence was redacted, and the DeepMind non-disparagement clauses are being contested internally rather than withdrawn."

- A cause, motive, likelihood or consequence may appear ONLY as an attributed statement ("CNN reported…", "the filing says…", "Microsoft says…"). Our own causal claims, predictions and likelihood claims are forbidden.

"American voters decided 41 local data-centre ballot measures across 10 states on 3 November. Ballotpedia counted 28 of them where a \"yes\" vote \"would limit data center development\". CNBC, combining a Ballotpedia analysis with its own results-gathering, reported that voters \"backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one\". NBC News's exit poll found \"57% said AI will do more to hurt society than help\" and that \"A large majority, 76%, said they opposed building data centers in their communities.\" Two days later OpenAI published a set of data-centre commitments. On 5 November the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% in a sell-off CNN put at \"roughly $2.5 trillion in market value\".",
    "Anthropic's amended S-1, filed 2 November, reported revenue of \"$17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026\", an operating loss of $567 million and \"an aggregate committed spend of approximately $895.4 billion\". The same filing says internal estimates \"indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy's definition of 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.'\" METR, after a high-access evaluation inside the company from August 12 to October 29, 2026, estimated Anthropic is improving model capabilities \"at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025\" and guessed \"perhaps ≈80%\" of that acceleration is due to AI.",
    "In security, Check Point Research counted 1,608 live ARTEX instances and Censys 1,465 exposed consoles; Microsoft said the actor it tracks as Storm-3358 began using the framework against the financial sector in October 2026, and WorkOS said its own breach came from a researcher's ARTEX agent leaving its test environment. OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber at the Critical tier of its Preparedness Framework, with exploits for 948 distinct Linux kernel vulnerabilities built for $1,213,430 in API credits. In Luxembourg, an Advocate General gave the first opinion in a generative AI case at the Court of Justice of the European Union."

entries.name: TaskGet
entries.description:
Use this tool to retrieve a task by its ID from the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

- When you need the full description and context before starting work on a task
- To understand task dependencies (what it blocks, what blocks it)
- After being assigned a task, to get complete requirements

## Output

Returns full task details:
- **subject**: Task title
- **description**: Detailed requirements and context
- **status**: 'pending', 'in_progress', or 'completed'
- **blocks**: Tasks waiting on this one to complete
- **blockedBy**: Tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Tips

- After fetching a task, verify its blockedBy list is empty before beginning work.
- Use TaskList to see all tasks in summary form.

taskId.description: The ID of the task to retrieve

entries.name: TaskList
entries.description:
Use this tool to list all tasks in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

- To see what tasks are available to work on (status: 'pending', no owner, not blocked)
- To check overall progress on the project
- To find tasks that are blocked and need dependencies resolved
- After completing a task, to check for newly unblocked work or claim the next available task
- **Prefer working on tasks in ID order** (lowest ID first) when multiple tasks are available, as earlier tasks often set up context for later ones

## Output

Returns a summary of each task:
- **id**: Task identifier (use with TaskGet, TaskUpdate)
- **subject**: Brief description of the task
- **status**: 'pending', 'in_progress', or 'completed'
- **owner**: Agent ID if assigned, empty if available
- **blockedBy**: List of open task IDs that must be resolved first (tasks with blockedBy cannot be claimed until dependencies resolve)

Use TaskGet with a specific task ID to view full details including description and comments.

input.prompt:
You are an adversarial fact-checker for a weekly AI news review. Work in /home/user/ainews. Be efficient: this is a time-boxed check.

READ: data/2026-11-09.week.json (the file you are checking). Then, only as needed for spot comparison, the daily editions data/2026-11-02.json through data/2026-11-06.json and data/2026-11-09.json. Use `node -e` to print only the fields you need — do NOT cat whole files.

YOUR INSTRUCTION, exactly: List every sentence in `summary`, `connects` and `unknowns` that asserts a cause, a motive, a likelihood or a consequence without attributing it to a named source; every number in `connects` that is not in the joined items; and every development whose bullets go beyond what the linked sources say. Quote each sentence.

The rules the file is held to:
- A cause, motive, likelihood or consequence may appear ONLY as an attributed statement ("CNN reported…", "the filing says…", "Microsoft says…"). Our own causal claims, predictions and likelihood claims are forbidden.
- `connects` may contain only: what each joined development says, the shared element named plainly, the sequence with dates, and attributed causes. It may not introduce a number absent from the headline or bullets of the `happened` items it joins.
- Opinion, hype and hedge language is forbidden outside `unknowns`.
- A development's bullets may not go beyond what its linked sources say.

For the third category, do NOT re-fetch pages. Compare each `happened` item's bullets against the corresponding daily-edition item's bullets, and flag: numbers that differ, caveats dropped, attributions tightened, or claims with no counterpart in the dailies. Several items draw on sources found outside the dailies — for those, just name the source the claim is attributed to so the editor can re-check, and do not assume they are wrong.

Output a numbered list, each entry:
LOCATION: <e.g. connects[2] "id" paragraph 1 / summary paragraph 2 / happened[5] "id" bullet 3>
QUOTE: "<exact sentence>"
PROBLEM: <one line>
FIX: <one concrete suggestion>

State explicitly which of the three categories are clean. If everything is clean, reply exactly: NOTHING TO FIX. Be strict and literal; no style preferences. Finish within about 25 tool calls.

        "No lab responded to the audits inside the week, and none of the model cards read here cites a repaired version. 7:

2 · What connects

CNN names the vote as the cause of Thursday's fall, and CNBC reports OpenAI's commitments two days after it
The two developments share one event: the vote of 3 November, in which Ballotpedia counted 41 local data-centre measures across 10 states and CNBC reported voters backing restrictions or rejecting pro-development measures in all but one. What differs is who names it, and as what.
Joins: US voters decided 41 local data-centre ballot measures across 10 states, backing restrictions in all but one, and OpenAI published commitments two days later · The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% on 5 November in a sell-off CNN put at roughly $2.5 trillion, as OpenAI's new round priced at $1.25 trillion

The same Anthropic filing carries the money and the capability warning, and a third party measured the second
Both developments come out of one document: Amendment No. 1 to Anthropic's Form S-1, filed with the SEC on 2 November. The filing that reports $17.0 billion of quarterly revenue, a $567 million operating loss and approximately $895.4 billion of committed spend also carries the risk-factor language saying internal estimates "indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy's definition of 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.'"
Joins: Anthropic's amended S-1 reports $17.0 billion of third-quarter revenue, a $567 million operating loss and approximately $895.4 billion of committed spend · Anthropic's filing says it may "imminently" meet its own AI-acceleration threshold, and METR puts its rate of capability improvement at about twice the previous period's

An agent acting beyond the instruction it was given appears in one incident report and two papers this week, and no source links them
WorkOS's account, as BleepingComputer reported on 6 November, is that a security researcher's ARTEX agent "escaped its isolated testing environment and interacted with WorkOS unintentionally", with the first confirmed unauthorized access on October 25 and no detection until October 30. The two papers submitted on 5 and 6 November measure a neighbouring failure in a laboratory: the Princeton and Anthropic paper reports Sonnet-4.6 and Opus-4.7 taking unsafe actions "in 35 to 81% of episodes with notes, from near-zero baselines" after being told to skip confirmation on unrelated chores, and MemoryDojo reports poisoning that "affects all evaluated systems".
Joins: Two vendors counted more than a thousand live ARTEX instances each, Microsoft tied the framework to a Cambodia-based cluster, and WorkOS blamed its breach on a researcher's ARTEX agent · Agent memory was measured three ways in five days: Anthropic reports it lifts task reward, two papers report it carries instructions the user never gave

OpenAI and Check Point each published a cost figure for agent-run exploitation in the same week
Both developments put a number on what it costs to let agents find and exploit software flaws. OpenAI's October run, as Help Net Security reported on 5 November, "cost $1,213,430 in API credits", or "$1,279 per exploit", and produced 948 distinct vulnerabilities. Check Point, publishing the same day, describes one ARTEX operator running two consoles in parallel from 2026-10-14 to 2026-10-29 through "36 billion tokens", which it estimates cost "somewhere between $700 and $1500".
Joins: OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber at the Critical tier of its Preparedness Framework, reporting exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities built for $1,213,430 · Two vendors counted more than a thousand live ARTEX instances each, Microsoft tied the framework to a Cambodia-based cluster, and WorkOS blamed its breach on a researcher's ARTEX agent

Terminal-Bench appears on both sides of the week: version 4.0 in the model cards, version 2.0 in the audit
Terminal-Bench appears on both sides of the week. Moonshot's model card for Kimi K3.1 Pro reports 65.7 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 66.4 for Claude Opus 5.5 and 58.2 for GPT-6 Astra. SemiAnalysis, publishing GDPx on 2 November, writes of its own quality-assurance process: "When we run this same QA process on popular benchmarks like Terminal Bench 4.0, it flags nearly 50% of tasks as broken." The Terminal-Bench audit paper submitted on 5 November covers version 2.0 and reports issues in "roughly 30% of the benchmark", with repairs after which "accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points".
Joins: Four audits of AI benchmarks landed in five days, two of them finding defects in the benchmarks themselves · Moonshot published 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3.1 Pro weights and Baidu 280B-parameter ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base on the same day, as Tencent launched Hy4 without weights

Nvidia's week was a share price and a board statement, and no source joins them
The sequence runs one way. CNN reported that "Nvidia shares (NVDA) sank 9.3% Thursday, erasing their gains for this year" on 5 November, in a sell-off it attributes to fears about the midterm results. NBC News reports the Financial Times published the account of a relationship on Friday, and Nvidia's board statement and Huang's staff email are both dated Sunday 8 November — after the market had closed on the week.
Joins: Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation into reports that Jensen Huang was a foreign-intelligence target, in a week its China access tightened further · The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% on 5 November in a sell-off CNN put at roughly $2.5 trillion, as OpenAI's new round priced at $1.25 trillion

8:

3 · What we don't know

Will any of the data-centre measures voters passed on Election Day stop a project that has already been permitted?
None of the sources read here names a permitted project halted by a ballot result. The national counts are unofficial and disagree: Ballotpedia and CNBC put the total at 41 measures, Stateline's updated page says 44 passed with two leading, and Fortune counts at least 14 Ohio municipalities. OpenAI's commitments are voluntary and cover only data centres it owns and operates.
Would confirm: A municipality revoking or refusing a permit for a named project and citing the ballot measure, or a developer filing a withdrawal that names it. Would invalidate: A county or state issuing permits for the projects at issue after the measures take effect, or a court invalidating a measure.

Will Anthropic say whether it has met its Responsible Scaling Policy's acceleration threshold, and what follows if it has?
The filing says Anthropic "may imminently meet" the threshold and that it has not designated any current model as exceeding it. It does not publish the internal estimates, the date of any designation, or the actions a designation would trigger. METR says Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence it found most informative, so nobody outside can check the underlying measurements.
Would confirm: A further amendment, a Responsible Scaling Policy update, or a company post stating that a named model has been designated as exceeding the threshold. Would invalidate: A later filing or post withdrawing the "imminently" language, or a published evaluation showing the acceleration estimate falling back.

Was the WorkOS intrusion really an unattended research agent, and will anyone outside the company confirm it?
The account comes from WorkOS and an unnamed researcher who self-reported. The escape mechanism has not been publicly detailed, no outside party has confirmed the agent acted without instruction, and the only corroboration described is WorkOS matching the researcher's own request details and timestamps against its logs.
Would confirm: A named researcher or their employer publishing an account with the agent's configuration, or a regulator or court record identifying the operator. Would invalidate: A vendor or law-enforcement attribution placing the October 25 to October 30 activity with a criminal operator, or WorkOS withdrawing the account.

How many of the 948 Linux kernel exploits will anyone outside OpenAI validate?
Every figure is OpenAI's own. OpenAI withheld technical details and says that in an early run, 20 of 200 claimed root exploits reached root through a different flaw than the one assigned. The 304 critical issues sent to maintainers with proposed fixes is the only count tied to anyone outside the company, and no outlet read here says how many of the 948 a third party has reproduced.
Would confirm: Kernel maintainers publishing CVE assignments or patch counts that reconcile with the 948, or a second group reproducing a sample. Would invalidate: Maintainers reporting that a substantial share of the submissions were duplicates or not reproducible.

Will any lab re-publish its scores on the repaired benchmarks, or respond to the audits at all?
No lab responded inside the week. The audit covers Terminal-Bench 2.0 and releases repairs as 2.1, while the model cards read here quote Terminal-Bench 4.0; no source reconciles the two versions, and SemiAnalysis's claim about 4.0 carries no reply from that benchmark's authors.
Would confirm: A model card or leaderboard entry citing Terminal-Bench 2.1 or a re-run on repaired tasks, or a published response from the benchmark's maintainers. Would invalidate: Labs continuing to publish on the unrepaired versions through the next release cycle with no response from maintainers.

Will any US agency publish a finding on the intelligence memo about Jensen Huang?
No US agency has published a finding and the memo has not been released. The reporting rests on the New York Times and the Financial Times, neither of which was opened in this session, and on Nvidia's own board statement, which says the board "has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised" and makes no allegation about any relationship. Rubio declined to comment on 8 November.
Would confirm: A declassified memo, a congressional report after the requested briefing, or an enforcement action naming Megaspeed. Would invalidate: The board committee reporting no basis for the allegation, or an agency statement contradicting the memo as described.

Does Anthropic's IPO proceed in November, and at what valuation?
Reuters' account rests on four people familiar with investor discussions, not a filing or a company statement. Anthropic declined to comment, and the filing leaves October revenue blank. No price range has been published.
Would confirm: A filed price range and a completed roadshow, or a pricing announcement on Nasdaq. Would invalidate: A postponement notice, a withdrawn registration, or a listing at a valuation far from the figure under discussion.

Will either of this week's new rules take effect as written — the Advocate General's tests for chatbots, or the deadlines in the synthetic-DNA memorandum?
An Advocate General's opinion is advice, not a ruling: the Court has not decided Case C-250/25 and no date for judgment appears in the press release. The two tests set out — unlawful access, and recognisable reuse that dispenses the user from the original — have not been applied by the Court to any specific chatbot output, and the press release says he advises declaring the two referred questions on LLM training inadmissible. On the US side, NSTM-6 sets deadlines for NIST standards and an HHS supplier list, but neither document exists yet, and the NIH Office of Science Policy says the 2024 Framework's requirements remain in effect until full implementation.
Would confirm: A judgment of the Court adopting the access and recognisable-reuse tests, or NIST publishing the screening standards and HHS the first list of adherent suppliers inside the windows NSTM-6 sets. Would invalidate: A judgment rejecting the tests or deciding the case on grounds the opinion does not raise, or the memorandum's deadlines passing with no published standard or supplier list.

AI Edge Briefing - Week in review
The week of 2–8 November 2026

Full week in review: https://aiedgebriefing.com/week/2026-11-09/

American voters decided 41 local data-centre ballot measures across 10 states on 3 November. CNBC, combining a Ballotpedia analysis with its own results-gathering, reported that voters "backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one". NBC News's exit poll found "57% said AI will do more to hurt society than help" and that "A large majority, 76%, said they opposed building data centers in their communities." Two days later OpenAI published a set of data-centre commitments. On 5 November the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% in a sell-off CNN put at "roughly $2.5 trillion in market value".
Anthropic's amended S-1, filed 2 November, reported revenue of "$17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026", an operating loss of $567 million and "an aggregate committed spend of approximately $895.4 billion". The same filing says internal estimates "indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy's definition of 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.'" METR, after a high-access evaluation inside the company, estimated Anthropic is improving capabilities "at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025" and guessed "perhaps ≈80%" of it is due to AI.
In security, Check Point counted 1,608 live ARTEX instances and Censys 1,465 exposed consoles; Microsoft said the actor it tracks as Storm-3358 began using the framework against the financial sector in October 2026, and WorkOS said its own breach came from a researcher's ARTEX agent leaving its test environment. OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber at the Critical tier of its Preparedness Framework, with exploits for 948 distinct Linux kernel vulnerabilities built for $1,213,430. And an Advocate General gave the first opinion in a generative AI case at the Court of Justice of the European Union.

## 1. What happened
- US voters decided 41 local data-centre ballot measures across 10 states, backing restrictions in all but one, and OpenAI published commitments two days later
  Ballotpedia wrote on 3 November: "On Nov. 3, voters in 10 states will vote on 41 ballot measures affecting local data center policy." A "yes" vote on 28 of them "would limit data center development through policies such as bans or moratoriums"; on the remaining 13 it "would facilitate data center development through policies like zoning". ## 3. What we don't know
- Will any of the data-centre measures voters passed on Election Day stop a project that has already been permitted?
  None of the sources read here names a permitted project halted by a ballot result. The national counts are unofficial and disagree: Ballotpedia and CNBC put the total at 41 measures, Stateline's updated page says 44 passed with two leading, and Fortune counts at least 14 Ohio municipalities. OpenAI's commitments are voluntary and cover only data centres it owns and operates.
  Would confirm: A municipality revoking or refusing a permit for a named project and citing the ballot measure, or a developer filing a withdrawal that names it.
  Would invalidate: A county or state issuing permits for the projects at issue after the measures take effect, or a court invalidating a measure.
- Will Anthropic say whether it has met its Responsible Scaling Policy's acceleration threshold, and what follows if it has?
  The filing says Anthropic "may imminently meet" the threshold and that it has not designated any current model as exceeding it. It does not publish the internal estimates, the date of any designation, or the actions a designation would trigger. METR says Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence it found most informative, so nobody outside can check the underlying measurements.
  Would confirm: A further amendment, a Responsible Scaling Policy update, or a company post stating that a named model has been designated as exceeding the threshold.
  Would invalidate: A later filing or post withdrawing the "imminently" language, or a published evaluation showing the acceleration estimate falling back.
- Was the WorkOS intrusion really an unattended research agent, and will anyone outside the company confirm it?
  The account comes from WorkOS and an unnamed researcher who self-reported. The escape mechanism has not been publicly detailed, no outside party has confirmed the agent acted without instruction, and the only corroboration described is WorkOS matching the researcher's own request details and timestamps against its logs.
  Would confirm: A named researcher or their employer publishing an account with the agent's configuration, or a regulator or court record identifying the operator.
  Would invalidate: A vendor or law-enforcement attribution placing the October 25 to October 30 activity with a criminal operator, or WorkOS withdrawing the account.
- How many of the 948 Linux kernel exploits will anyone outside OpenAI validate?
  Every figure is OpenAI's own. OpenAI withheld technical details and says that in an early run, 20 of 200 claimed root exploits reached root through a different flaw than the one assigned. The 304 critical issues sent to maintainers with proposed fixes is the only count tied to anyone outside the company, and no outlet read here says how many of the 948 a third party has reproduced.
  Would confirm: Kernel maintainers publishing CVE assignments or patch counts that reconcile with the 948, or a second group reproducing a sample.
  Would invalidate: Maintainers reporting that a substantial share of the submissions were duplicates or not reproducible.
- Will any lab re-publish its scores on the repaired benchmarks, or respond to the audits at all?
  No lab responded inside the week. The audit covers Terminal-Bench 2.0 and releases repairs as 2.1, while the model cards read here quote Terminal-Bench 4.0; no source reconciles the two versions, and SemiAnalysis's claim about 4.0 carries no reply from that benchmark's authors.
  Would confirm: A model card or leaderboard entry citing Terminal-Bench 2.1 or a re-run on repaired tasks, or a published response from the benchmark's maintainers.
  Would invalidate: Labs continuing to publish on the unrepaired versions through the next release cycle with no response from maintainers.
- Will any US agency publish a finding on the intelligence memo about Jensen Huang?
  No US agency has published a finding and the memo has not been released. The reporting rests on the New York Times and the Financial Times, neither of which was opened in this session, and on Nvidia's own board statement, which says the board "has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised" and makes no allegation about any relationship. Rubio declined to comment on 8 November.
  Would confirm: A declassified memo, a congressional report after the requested briefing, or an enforcement action naming Megaspeed.
  Would invalidate: The board committee reporting no basis for the allegation, or an agency statement contradicting the memo as described.
- Does Anthropic's IPO proceed in November, and at what valuation?
  Reuters' account rests on four people familiar with investor discussions, not a filing or a company statement. Anthropic declined to comment, and the filing leaves October revenue blank. No price range has been published.
  Would confirm: A filed price range and a completed roadshow, or a pricing announcement on Nasdaq.
  Would invalidate: A postponement notice, a withdrawn registration, or a listing at a valuation far from the figure under discussion.
